rationale: The exact BOOK ENTRY identifies sin by the explicit definitional clause in 1 John 3:4 and the three supporting Romans texts that tie the existence, knowledge, and possibility of sin/transgression to law. Those four texts carry the printed claims without remainder. The common broader readings (missing the mark, rebellion, fallen condition, enslaving power, etc.) incorporate or presuppose the same legal identification rather than contradicting it; they therefore function as SAME_CORE_BROADER elaborations, not as superior rival cores for the supplied definitional evidence. No material assertion printed in the entry is left unsupported, and no supplied text is better explained by denying the entry’s core.
book_core_identification: Sin is the transgression of the law—Scripture’s own definition.
book_secondary_elaborations: Where no law is, there is no transgression.
By the law is the knowledge of sin.
chapter_only_objections: Chapter applications equating ‘sin no more’ strictly with resumed Torah-keeping, the willful/unintentional division as the decisive soteriological hinge, and the claim that denying the law insults the Spirit of grace go beyond the glossary entry’s definitional scope.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Sin primarily denotes the broader moral and relational reality of rebellion against God, falling short of His glory, and the resultant alienated/fallen condition (with law-transgression as one prominent manifestation or the instrument by which sin is known, not the exhaustive definition).
counter_core_identification: Sin is rebellion/falling short/alienation from God (lawlessness being a key but non-exhaustive aspect).
material_core_denial: The counter does not deny that sin is (or includes) transgression of the law; it only embeds that identification inside a wider set of metaphors and conditions.
counter_case: Romans 3:23 frames sin as falling short of God’s glory rather than solely as discrete legal breaches.
Romans 5–7 and Genesis 3 portray sin as an entering power/condition and Adamic inheritance, not merely individual transgressions.
Multiple metaphors (debt, disease, stain, slavery) appear alongside the legal language and are treated as complementary in the common tradition.
book_explanatory_advantages: Directly quotes and rests on the only verse that offers an explicit ‘sin is …’ definition (1 John 3:4 KJV).
The three Romans texts supply the precise logical corollaries printed in the entry (no law 	o no transgression; law 	o knowledge of sin).
Requires no extra-textual synthesis; the entry is essentially a concatenation of the four cited clauses.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Accounts for the wider range of Pauline and narrative language (power, inheritance, glory-falling-short) that the narrow legal formula does not independently generate.
Matches the multi-metaphor consensus across historic Christian traditions.
